tone_statements.quote: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable.[fn 28] It is not phonemic, nor are there any other suprasegmental features with phonemic relevance. [fn 28:] Van der Toorn (not specifying whether this applies to lexemes or to words) speaks of a slightly longer penultimate vowel (Van der Toorn 1899:XIV). Moussay (1981) does not comment on MIN stress.

tone_statements.summary: Penultimate, non-phonemic, no schwa exception stated for MIN; confirms the catalog's fixed penultimate rule and no-tone class; the footnote leans on the catalog's own source (Van der Toorn 1899: XIV, longer penultimate vowel), so not independent.

audit.recode_to: Keep penult as the reported pattern but add a caution/contested flag: 'word stress disputed — van der Toorn 1899 denies intensity differences (penult only slightly longer, mainly when open); Gil 2006 and Crouch 2009:235 (preliminary acoustics) find intonation-unit-final prominence and no conclusive word-level penult effect; penult per Adelaar 1992:12/1995:437 and Zarbaliev 1987:23'. If the catalog has a Malay/Indonesian-type 'contested / possibly no word stress' class, Minangkabau belongs in it rather than plain fixed-dominant.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding van der Toorn 1899 §3 passage is present verbatim (scanned-normalized) in the djvu text we hold at p. XIV, and the phrase-stress continuation at p. XV supports the existing word and phrase together-domain correction. sources.quote: "The relation of tone-intensity between the different syllables of a polysyllabic word — the syllable-tone — as it occurs in Dutch, does not exist in Minangkabau. In this language the tone-strength is the same for every syllable of a word, whether it consists of closed or open syllables or both, and this for both root words and derivations. ... In pronouncing a word, however, some difference can be observed in the duration with which the syllables are held: namely, the penultimate syllable sound
